summary:
Fire behaves differently in space. Without gravity-driven convection, flames can take unfamiliar shapes, spread in unexpected ways, and create risks that are difficult to study under normal conditions. For astronauts living and working hundreds of kilometres above Earth, understanding these risks is a matter of safety.

FlameAtlas, developed by Team TerraFlame for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, is an interactive platform that makes microgravity fire research easier to explore and understand. It brings NASA research and space science data together through 3D flame visualizations, spacecraft fire simulations, an AI-powered research assistant, material risk analysis, and live solar flare monitoring using NASA's DONKI data.

By connecting scientific findings with interactive scenarios, FlameAtlas helps users understand how factors such as oxygen levels, pressure, gravity, and material properties influence fire behaviour. Our aim is to turn complex research into something people can actually explore, question, and learn from—contributing to a better understanding of fire safety as humanity moves towards longer and more ambitious space missions.
details:
FlameAtlas is an interactive platform developed by Team TerraFlame for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It focuses on one important question: how does fire behave in space, and what does that mean for the safety of astronauts and spacecraft?

Research on combustion in microgravity is spread across NASA experiments, technical reports, scientific papers, and datasets. Finding relevant information and understanding how different conditions affect fire can be difficult. FlameAtlas brings this information together in one place and makes it easier to explore through interactive visualizations, simulations, and an AI-powered research assistant.

The platform includes several main features. Flame Lab lets users explore how flames behave under different gravity and environmental conditions. The spacecraft simulation allows users to experiment with fire-related emergency scenarios and observe how conditions such as oxygen levels, pressure, and materials can affect the situation. FireGPT acts as a research assistant, helping users find and understand information grounded in NASA research. The Material Risk Ranker helps compare spacecraft materials based on fire-related risk factors, while the Solar Flare Watcher presents space-weather information using NASA's DONKI data. A research-gap feature also helps highlight areas where available evidence is limited.

Our goal was not to build an autonomous fire-control system or claim that our simulations can predict real spacecraft emergencies. Instead, we wanted to make existing research easier to understand and provide an interactive environment for learning, exploration, and preliminary risk assessment. By connecting scientific findings with practical scenarios, FlameAtlas can support students, researchers, and anyone interested in space exploration and fire safety.

We built the project as a web application using HTML, Tailwind CSS, Alpine.js, JavaScript, Three.js, GSAP, and Chart.js. The backend uses Node.js and Vercel serverless functions, with an OpenAI API integration supporting the research assistant. We also used NASA research repositories, technical publications, and the DONKI API as reference sources. No specialised hardware was required; the platform runs in a web browser.

What makes FlameAtlas different is how it combines scientific research, 3D visualisation, interactive simulations, and AI-assisted exploration into a single platform. Rather than presenting research as a collection of documents, it gives users ways to interact with the concepts and understand how different variables can influence fire behaviour.

Throughout development, we considered scientific credibility, source traceability, usability, and the limitations of the available research. We wanted the platform to distinguish between NASA-backed findings and our own prototype simulations, while keeping the experience accessible to people without a specialised background in combustion science. Ultimately, we hope FlameAtlas makes space-fire research more accessible and contributes to better understanding of one of the safety challenges involved in future human space exploration.
